about: Hand-kept: the stages of paper 1's production, the checklist before prose, and the journal. The numbers live in ledger.json (generated); this file says what has been done and what hasn't. The process page (four/papers/) renders both.

paper.title: Atoms in four spatial dimensions with a 1/r interaction: a self-consistent periodic table
paper.status: in preparation: restructured around the charge law; seven figures and the methods drafted; the counterfactual table queued
paper.bar: arXiv's: checkable claims, verified references, reproducible numbers. Every number in the text comes from a baked file and is checked against it.

authors.name: Astra
authors.role: independent audit: the failure contracts behind selftest 58, and the audit rounds for this paper
authors.note: the form of credit (author, audit appendix or acknowledgement) is still to settle

authors.name: minor mobius
authors.role: direction, judgement of results, PI (last author)

authorship_note: arXiv doesn't accept AI models as authors. If the paper goes there, the byline is minor mobius and the AI contributors move to a contribution statement, with the session record. On four.mino.mobi the byline above stands.

pipeline.name: The solver
pipeline.what: atom.js: the radial equation with l + (D − 3)/2, Numerov on a log grid, a self-consistent field with Hartree and local exchange, the ground-configuration search

pipeline.name: The bake
pipeline.what: every element in both worlds, solved once (on the runner for Z past ~80) and frozen: configurations, energies, orbitals, densities

pipeline.name: The gates
pipeline.what: the selftest's blocks recompute a sample of the bake and check each method against closed forms and published values; block 67 checks the paper's own data and every claim in its ledger

pipeline.name: The law calculations
pipeline.what: one electron under Gauss's 1/r² (no atom: nothing binds, or it falls to the centre) and under 1/r^p (only p = 1 keeps a shell together)

pipeline.name: The solver audit
pipeline.what: the bake's stop against one a hundred-thousandfold tighter, on 19 atoms across every row of both worlds: what in the table is converged and what isn't

pipeline.name: Data and ledger
pipeline.what: the paper's tables as JSON and CSV, each figure's data, and the ledger of claims, all generated from the bake

pipeline.name: References
pipeline.what: one entry per source, marked read, index, cited or memory; checked against Crossref; only read and index may be cited

pipeline.name: Reproduction
pipeline.what: re-solves a sample of the paper's atoms from the solver and matches the data to the bit; ships in the open mirror

pipeline.name: The counterfactual table
pipeline.what: every element solved again with the shell theorem forced on, everything else held: what the table owes to the law rather than to the geometry
pipeline.note: 112 of 140 settled after lawtable-repair; row 6's f block (89–116) has no settled ground state under the shell theorem

pipeline.name: Widgets
pipeline.what: screening on and off, solved live; a neutral atom's far pull

pipeline.name: Figures
pipeline.what: SVG drawn from the bake and the law code by a script on every build, never by hand (Okabe–Ito palette, the shared library's theme); captions beside them in the same file
pipeline.note: pruned to six for the main text and two for the appendix; 6 waits on the counterfactual run

pipeline.name: The text
pipeline.what: each section's source with every number a token the build fills from the code or the bake; an unknown token stops the build
pipeline.note: methods and part I (the law, sections 2–4) drafted and rendered

pipeline.name: The paper page
pipeline.what: each draft section rendered by pandoc with its maths as MathML (browsers draw it natively, no maths library downloaded) on the paper stylesheet forked from wormhole's; a page carries its source's hash, so the selftest catches a stale one
pipeline.note: methods rendered; the full assembled paper is to come

pipeline.name: Open code
pipeline.what: the solvers, the reproduction and the data, MIT, on tangled; staged and tested on every push
pipeline.note: the repo has to be created on tangled by its owner

pipeline.name: Audit
pipeline.what: Astra's rounds on the paper's claims and code

checklist.item: Before the paper is assembled: every author–year in the text must be a read or index reference. Part I cites Ehrenfest 1917, still only cited
checklist.note: Ehrenfest 1917 confirmed via indexes (read 26 May 1917, Proc. Amsterdam 20, 1918); 1920 via a scan of the original

checklist.item: The counterfactual table: run lawtable-shell, bake it, add its claims, and say whether the generalized Madelung rows come from the law or from the geometry alone
checklist.note: 112 of 140 settled: rows the geometry's through row 5, the d-and-f order and the binding the law's; 89–116 don't settle under the shell theorem (next: a homotopy from the law's converged field)

checklist.item: Element 128 out-holds its row's noble gas: is it partial screening? Read it off the counterfactual table
checklist.note: yes, the law: 3.1 eV with the shell theorem against 29.6 under the law

checklist.item: Choose the title: the table first, or the law first
checklist.note: left to the end, with the abstract (the PI may write it by hand)

checklist.item: Find citable sources for Hardy's inequality in D dimensions and the fall to the centre (Landau–Lifshitz §35, to check)
checklist.note: Landau–Lifshitz §35 'Fall of a particle to the centre' (3rd ed. contents); Hardy's constant via Barbatis, arXiv:2311.08017

checklist.item: Forward citation search on Pyykkö & Zhao (1991) and Négadi & Kibler (1996) in a citation index, for any later self-consistent table at D = 4
checklist.note: a web search found none; the paper says "to our knowledge" until an index search is run

checklist.item: Turn every cited reference into read or index
checklist.note: 28 of 30: madelung1936 (the rule's page) and nist-asd (the promotion energies) remain

checklist.item: Solver audit: atom.js's self-consistent field stops on the total energy. Check whether that leaves the far density unconverged, and what it does to the table's energies and ionizations
checklist.note: 19 atoms, both worlds, stop 10⁻⁷ → 10⁻¹² hartree: energies and ionizations move ≤ 3 × 10⁻⁷ hartree, Σ⟨r²⟩ ≤ 2 × 10⁻⁵ relative. The far tail is unconverged only where it is noise (10⁻¹³ electrons per bohr and below). Nothing quoted depends on it.

checklist.item: Convergence runs for appendix C: grid (N, r₀, r_max), SCF tolerance, a few elements per row
checklist.note: 11 atoms, both worlds, six grids (N 500/1000, r₀ 10⁻⁴/10⁻⁶, r_max 100/250): ionizations move ≤ 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ hartree, total energies ≤ 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ of themselves (worst: our krypton's deep 1s)

checklist.item: Re-derive the 3D validation from the current bake
Decide the Z range in the main text: to 78 with 79–140 marked first-pass, or all 140 with the relativistic caveat
The equation pipeline: KaTeX pre-rendering in the sandbox, or hand-written MathML
Tag the mirror version the paper cites

The term-corrected table (termtable.mjs, runner run hund-f-and-terms): which elements change configuration, how far the ionizations move; make it the main table (data, figures, section 8 tokens) and move the Hund-spin table to supplement S1
checklist.note: no configuration changes from the terms; 8 ionizations ±0.30–0.67 eV; element 82 corrected by the wider search; main table now, S1 = Hund-spin

checklist.item: Hund's rule over the rest of the 4D f block (4f⁵–4f³¹, elements 85–110, runner); fold into data/hund.json (hund-collect.mjs) and section 7.2
checklist.note: 4f²⁹ (108) breaks it too (0.26 eV); every other filling holds (bounds for f⁶–f²⁵); 102 and 106 unfinished

checklist.item: Prior art on Hund's rules in D dimensions: three web searches found none; run a citation-index search before the paper calls section 7 new
Section 8.2 quotes palladium 8.3 eV and xenon 12.1 eV from memory: cite a measured source (NIST ASD)
checklist.note: NIST Handbook: Pd 8.3369 eV, Xe 12.1298 eV

checklist.item: Introduction and abstract, written last against the finished Parts I–III
checklist.note: text/intro.md; the whole draft assembled as draft/paper.{md,html,pdf}

checklist.item: The site's own table chapter and js/table.js still show the bake (element 82 as 4f² 6s², the Hund-spin energies): rebake with the term-corrected search, or overlay data/termtable.json on the site
checklist.note: atom/tools/terms.mjs bakes js/terms.js; js/tablec.js lays it over the bake; every page reads the table from tablec.js; selftest 69 checks it against data/termtable.json

checklist.item: Check the measured 4s→3d promotion energies (section 6.3) and Pd/Xe ionizations (8.2) against NIST ASD and cite with the access date

journal.what: The write-up pinned: a kit survey of what the repo already had for a paper, and the decision that writing waits while the science moves. The literature register opened, each source tagged by how far it had been checked.

A lesson from elsewhere in the project: the plane-wave code's pseudopotentials were wrong because their all-electron atom stopped iterating on its eigenvalues while its far density was still unsettled. The atom solver behind this paper stops on its total energy. That goes on the checklist as an audit, not an assumption.
Writing started. The outline maps every claim to the baked file and the selftest block that hold it up; the figure plan and the companion objects are listed with it.

The data release and its gate: build.mjs writes the tables, the figure data and a ledger of claims from the bake, and selftest 67 fails if any of it goes stale or any claim stops holding. Re-deriving the 3D check gave 32 of 36 configurations (Ti, V, Co and Ni each put one electron too many in 3d) and a 4.3 % median ionization error.

The references checked against Crossref. It corrected four entries the register had from memory or from other papers' citations: Al-Jaber's volume and pages, Loos & Gill's, Kventsel & Katriel's title (it's the Thomas–Fermi atom in N dimensions), and Loeser & Herschbach 1986, which is two papers: the exact energies at 84, 3882 and Hartree–Fock at 84, 3893.

The reproduction: a script that re-solves a sample of the paper's atoms with the bake's own function. 14 of 14 matched the data to the bit, in 18 s on four cores. It ships in the open mirror, whose workflow runs it on every push.

Two widgets. Screening on and off solves any 4D atom live, with and without the shell theorem, and gives back the bake's numbers (element 12 holds its outer electron at 18.39 eV against 10.30; element 138 at 26.71 against 9.22). The far pull walks an electron away from a neutral atom; the full cloud meets −S/8s³ to within a fraction of a percent past 20 bohr.
This page: the paper's production made public as it happens, its claims recomputed from the bake on every build.

Restructured around the charge law, at the PI's direction: the choice of law, why it has to be made and what it costs are now the first part of the paper, and the table is measured against a counterfactual. New ledger claims, computed: Gauss's 1/r² in 4D binds nothing below α = ½ and falls to the centre above it (the ground level scales as 1/r₀² with the grid's inner end, constant to four figures over three decades); among power laws only 1/r keeps 2s with 2p (10⁻¹¹; −6 % at p = 0.8, +15 % at p = 1.2); ∇²(1/r) = −1/r³; k(1) = 8/3π. Five references for the law confirmed on Crossref.

A first look at the counterfactual, in the sandbox: with the shell theorem forced on, element 26 settles in 4s² 4p² instead of 3d² 4s² (even when seeded with the real configuration) and its ionization halves; element 100 fills its f shell to 4f³⁰ before 5p. The law doesn't just tighten the binding: it decides where the blocks begin. The full table is queued on the runner.

Seven figures, drawn from the bake and the law code by a script that runs with every build (so a stale figure fails the selftest like a stale number): Gauss's law's fall to the centre, the shell splitting against the exponent, the 3-sphere kernel, ionization against Z in both worlds, the 3D validation, partial screening, and the far pull.

The first figure of ionization against Z showed what the outline had wrong: the hardest-held electron in the 4D table isn't a noble gas's. Element 128, a full 18-electron d shell with nothing outside it (our palladium's kind), holds its outermost electron at 29.56 eV against its row's noble gas 138 at 26.71; element 68, the same kind a row up, comes within a volt of its row's. In ours palladium holds far less hard than xenon. A first wording of the claim said 68 also beat its row's noble gas; the ledger's own value showed it doesn't (22.32 against 78's 23.10), and the claim was corrected before it went in. Whether partial screening causes this is a question for the counterfactual.

The methods section drafted. Its numbers (grid, tolerances, mixing, the kernel's quadrature, the exchange constants, the search's rounds) are tokens the build reads from the solver's own source, so the text says what the code does.

The figures pruned, at the PI's direction: half of the first seven only illustrated. The main text now has six: the table itself; the choice of law (Gauss's fall to the centre beside the shell splitting against the exponent); orbitals only four dimensions has, cut through the nucleus by a plane on solved atoms' radial functions (the fourth p orbital along w, and a d orbital positive all round one plane and negative all round its completely perpendicular one); ionization against Z; six elements in profile; and the counterfactual (a stand-in until its run). The kernel and our-world validation moved to the appendix; the far-pull curve, the α scan and the shell's potential were cut. The six profiled atoms are the bake's own, re-solved with their radial functions kept; the build stops if one drifts from the bake.

The solver audit, the methods section's one open item: 19 atoms across every row of both worlds re-solved and driven from the bake's stop (energy change under 10⁻⁷ hartree) to one under 10⁻¹². Total and ionization energies moved by at most 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ hartree (8 μeV), Σ⟨r²⟩ by 2 × 10⁻⁵ of itself. The far density is not converged relatively past about 15 bohr, but only where it is noise, 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁷ electrons per bohr; atoms with a loose s electron, which do put charge out there, are converged to 10⁻⁶. So the plane-wave bug's lesson doesn't touch the table: it bites what builds a potential from the far density through exchange, which the pseudopotentials now converge pointwise. A new ledger claim holds it.

The kit, re-surveyed: pandoc 3.1.3 is now in the sandbox (the survey found none), which turns the text's maths into MathML that browsers render natively and writes the LaTeX source arXiv compiles itself, so the paper needs neither a downloaded maths library nor a local TeX. Still no TeX engine; KaTeX is fetchable but not needed.

The counterfactual answered part III's question. With the shell theorem forced on, the first 24 elements and all six noble gases come out the same, so the rows the generalized Madelung rule predicts are the geometry's (four-dimensional shells), not the law's. What the law decides is everything inside the rows from the first d element on: 52 of the 107 atoms that settled change configuration, every one from element 25, because without the law p beats d; outer electrons are held a median 2.5 times harder under the law; and element 128's record 29.6 eV falls to 3.1, the noble gases holding hardest as ours do. In every changed atom the law's own configuration still comes out lower under the law, so the comparison holds both ways.

And what the counterfactual didn't settle, caught before it went in: for 33 atoms (38, 39, 41, 88–117) no candidate's field converged, and the search reports an unsettled filling with no energy. A first count had all 84 differing configurations as results; 33 of them were those fillings. Counted honestly it is 52 of 107. One unsettled filling, element 110 as 4f³² 5s² 5p⁸, is a closed shell, which would split row 6 if it held, so 'the rows are the geometry's' waits on a wider re-search with gentler mixing (lawtable-repair, queued; element 38 settled in two minutes in the sandbox).

pw-fixed came in (the 3D check of the plane-wave code, for the molecules paper): corundum lowest and the order right, θ within 0.11 eV of same-functional PySCF, but the impostor 0.26 and poly6 0.40 off, against the 0.2 eV bar agreed. The stop-loss applies there; it doesn't touch paper 1.

The counterfactual's repair run: of the 33 atoms that hadn't settled, a wider search (every configuration in reach, mixing 0.15, 1500 iterations) settled 38, 39, 41, 88 and 117 (38–41 again put an electron in 4p rather than 3d). Three more, 114–116, 'settled' on configurations an electron would rather leave (negative ionization energies): the search missed lower ones, so they don't count. The other 25, 89–113, the heart of row 6's f block, don't converge at all under the shell theorem. Every atom up to 88 is now settled, so the rows are the geometry's through row 5; whether the shell theorem would close a shell at 110 and split row 6 stays open. Next: follow each atom from the law's converged field to the shell theorem's in small steps of the kernel, instead of searching.

Methods finished as a draft. Grid convergence, appendix C's promise: 11 atoms from every row of both worlds re-solved on six other grids (half and twice the points, the inner end ten times out or in, the outer end at 100 or 250 bohr). No ionization moved by more than 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ hartree (4 meV); total energies by at most a few parts per million, the worst our own krypton, whose 1s is deeper than any 4D atom's. A new ledger claim holds it. The counterfactual's paragraph now says how atoms that wouldn't settle were searched again and what counts as settled. And the methods section is the first rendered page of the paper: pandoc turns its maths into MathML on a stylesheet forked from wormhole's journal pages.

Part I drafted: why a law has to be chosen (Gauss's law in four dimensions has no atom: Hardy's floor, and the computed fall to the centre), the ways out and what each costs, why 1/r exactly (the only power law that keeps a shell together), and what it costs in four dimensions (not harmonic, no shell theorem or Faraday cage, the five routes to a field theory and the lens vacuum this universe takes, what is declared alongside, and the evidence that matter is stable). Every number in it is read from the ledger or the code. One new claim backs the stability section: the solved table's total energies follow each world's Thomas–Fermi law, a fitted exponent of 2.53 in four dimensions against 5/2, and 2.39 in ours against 7/3.

Hund's first rule doesn't hold in four dimensions, and the paper now says so. A crystal-field side project turned up the free 4D d² ion with a spin-singlet ground term. A survey of every open subshell in the table (tools/hund.mjs: degree-l harmonics on the 3-sphere, the law projected onto them, every M_S block by Lanczos) finds that it fails for d² and d¹⁶ in all three d rows (elements 26, 39, 54, 66, 114, 126, by 0.30–0.77 eV) and for 4f³ (element 83). It holds for every p filling, every other d filling, 4f² and 4f⁴, and for every open subshell of our own table. It isn't the law: Gauss's 1/r² gives the same order on the same orbital. The PI's call: the table corrected for it (tools/termtable.mjs, now on the runner) becomes the main table, and the Hund-spin table moves to a supplement. Parts II and III drafted around it: checks against what is known (6), Hund's rule in four dimensions (7), the table (8), the counterfactual (9), partial screening (10), neutral atoms (11), limitations (12) and the conclusion (13). Four new ledger claims back section 7 (hund3, hund4, hund4f3, hundlaw), 23 in all, every one holding.

Why Hund's rule breaks, made exact, and an explainer for it. For two d electrons every term's energy is F⁰ + a₂F² + a₄F⁴, where a₂ measures how much the term lets the two electrons line up. In 4D the ten-state singlet keeps them nearest right angles (⟨cos²γ⟩ 1/8, half of random; the best triplet 0.19). It lies below every triplet whenever F⁴/F² < 5/3; element 26 sits at 0.39 under the law and 0.65 under Gauss's. In ours ³F wins for every value. Section 7.3 rewritten around it, with a 24th ledger claim (hundcrit). The interactive version is four.mino.mobi/atom/hund.html: orbitals as boxes, the d orbitals on the sphere and on slices of the 3-sphere, the pair's separation-angle distribution for every term, the level ladder against F⁴/F² with real atoms marked, and the survey across the table.

The f block surveyed (runner run hund-f). 4f³'s mirror 4f²⁹ (element 108) breaks Hund's rule too, by 0.26 eV, spin ½. Every other f filling keeps it: completely for f², f⁴, f⁵, f²⁸ and f³⁰, and for f⁶–f²⁵ over the highest two or three spins, the lower-spin blocks running to 10⁶–10⁸ arrangements, so a bound. Elements 102 and 106 didn't finish. So in four dimensions the rule breaks two from either end of the d shell and three from either end of the f shell, and nowhere else surveyed. Ledger claim hund4f29 makes 25, all holding.

The term-corrected table is in (runner run hund-f-and-terms, 92 d- and f-block elements searched again with neighbour seeds, every candidate corrected for its open subshells' Hund gaps) and is now the paper's main table. The Hund-spin bake is supplement S1 (data/table4-hundspin.*). The terms change no ground configuration. They lower the eight Hund-breaking atoms' energies and move eight first ionizations, in pairs, by 0.30–0.67 eV: up for 54, 66, 114, 126, down for the next element, whose ion lands on the broken filling (55, 67, 115, 127). The wider search found one configuration the bake had missed: element 82 is 4f¹ 5d¹ 6s² (our cerium's kind), 0.36 eV below 4f² 6s². Rows, noble gases, element 128's lead and the 2.54 hold ratio are untouched. Ledger claim termtable makes 26, all holding; §7.4 and a methods paragraph written.

The full term correction, tested and rejected. Beyond Hund's first rule, the solver also averages every open subshell over orbitals, so we tried correcting each candidate by its whole term structure: lowest term less the average of the maximum-spin arrangements. That average has a closed form, checked against brute force. Tested on ours first (TERM_MODE=full, elements 5–36): it fixes none of the four misses and breaks two that were right (Sc, Fe), 26 of 32 against 28. The 4s→3d promotion energies against measured ones show why. The solver comes out too cheap for d in every 3d atom, by 0.35–1.70 eV, a mean 1.06 (local exchange without correlation), and the full correction leaves that mean where it is (1.07). So the paper corrects only Hund's first rule, the one thing a spin-polarized averaged field cannot represent, and states the bias. It also gives a robustness measure: 11 of the 92 4D d- and f-block elements have a fewer-d competitor within a volt (element 53's is 0.01 eV). New data/promotion3.json (promotion-collect.mjs), ledger claim promotion (27, all holding), §6.3, §7.4 and §12 updated, reference nist-asd added (from memory, to verify).

The first whole draft. The abstract and introduction are written (text/intro.md), last, against Parts I–III as they stand. The build now assembles the whole paper as draft/paper.md: abstract and introduction, Part I, the methods as section 5 opening Part II, Parts II and III, the figures with their captions, what is still to write, and the references. It renders to draft/paper.html and prints to draft/paper.pdf (pdf.cjs, headless Chromium, A4). Four references were checked against indexes and sources: Ehrenfest 1917 and 1920 (a scan of the 1920 original), Landau–Lifshitz §35, and Hardy's constant (Barbatis's review). Palladium's and xenon's ionization energies match NIST's tables (nist-handbook), so 28 of 30 references are now citable. Still from memory: the 4s→3d promotion energies (NIST ASD), and the page of Madelung's 1936 book that carries the rule. Working title, law first, pending the PI's call.

The PI's call: no title and no abstract until the end, and the abstract may be hand-written. Both are now placeholders in the whole draft. The papers page leads with a 'read the current draft' link (draft/paper.html, and the PDF). The appendices are written (text/appendix.md): A, the 4D kernel; B, the 4D electron gas; C, numerical convergence (a table of the six grids); D, the law calculations; E, reproducing every number (every data file, what made it and where). A turned up a closed form, k(t) = 4[(1 + t²)E(t) − (1 − t²)K(t)]/3πt² in complete elliptic integrals, equal to the solver's quadrature to 3 × 10⁻¹⁵; ledger claim kernelclosed makes 28, all holding.

Ions (runner run ions-1: every cation and anion of both worlds searched for its own ground state, 350 searches, all exit 0). In ours the cation search changes no ionization. The anion search gets all seven unbound anions unbound and every p-block acceptor bound (C 1.32 against 1.26, Ge 1.25 against 1.23, F 2.80 against 3.40). It fails where correlation binds (H⁻, the alkalis, P, As), so in 4D an affinity above about 0.7 eV is believed. In 4D, element 128's 29.56 eV survives. Seven ions rearrange (36, 93–95, 103–105), lowering those ionizations by up to 1.29 eV, and the main table carries them. A new result: one electron short of a full 4D p shell, atoms hold an extra electron harder and harder down the group (3.4, 5.7, 7.8, 10.3, 12.9 eV) where ours stay level near 3.4, partial screening again (§10.3). 80 of 140 bind an extra electron by more than 0.7 eV; the light noble gases don't, the heavy ones come out barely bound. New: data/ions.json (ions-collect.mjs), an electron_affinity_eV column, three claims (ions3, ions4, halogens4), 31 in all, holding.

Editorial pass on Part I after the PI's read of sections 1–4. Explanations replace the oracles: §2.1 now derives the collapse (the Hamiltonian's scale symmetry; r^σ near the origin, σ = −1 ± √(1 − 2α), complex past α = ½, so infinitely many nodes and no lowest level) and names the solver (laws.js: Numerov on a log grid, node-count bisection); §3.1 explains the hidden symmetry (Bertrand's closed orbits, the Runge–Lenz vector, SO(D + 1) from Fock's momentum-space sphere, why only 1/r: its Fourier transform 1/k^(D−1) is Gauss's kernel one dimension up) and answers 'why not 1.5' (it binds with a size, but 2p sits 64% of the shell's binding above 2s, so no shells); §4.1–4.2 give the flux and the mean-value reasons; §4.3 explains each route and says the paper uses only the lens vacuum's statics, its dynamics being the later paper; the □ (which rendered as a white box) is now the wave operator written out. References are pandoc citations through citeproc, author–date, each linked to its entry and each entry to its DOI; metadata from Crossref (refs-crossref.mjs → data/crossref.json), with new DOIs for Ehrenfest 1920, Herschbach et al. (1993), Barbatis (2024), Landau–Lifshitz, Sansonetti–Martin and Rienstra-Kiracofe (now index), and Ehrenfest 1917 read from the KNAW scan (Proc. 20, 1918, 200–209). A notation table (text/notation.md) follows the introduction, and the symbols are unified: the trial exponent is η (was p, which is momentum), the shell kernel κ (was k, which is wavenumber), the atom's second moment Q (was S, which is spin), the exchange constant A_D (was C_D, beside the Gegenbauer C_n), fields bold, electron mass m_e, the nonlinear exponent β, elliptic integrals upright. A section 5 subsection, 'The code', says what computes everything.
